A starting point, not a policy. {#tbl-practical-consumer-actions} The last row deserves emphasis. A navigation process that has crashed publishes no health message announcing the fact, so every consumer needs its own **watchdog** on the age of the newest state it has received. Inside the estimator, watchdogs check the time since the last IMU sample and since each aid, the fraction of measurements rejected by gating, covariance growth beyond configured bounds, missed deadlines, and NaN or invalid-state events. The fallback does not have to be glamorous: hold position, slow down, return control to a human, use attitude-only stabilization, or coast briefly on the IMU. The unacceptable behavior is silently publishing a confident state after the estimator has evidence that it is unhealthy. ## Real-Time Execution and Numerical Health {#sec-practical-real-time-execution} A real-time navigation package has timing budgets. Approximate values: | Component | Typical rate | Practical concern | |---|---:|---| | IMU propagation | 100–1000 Hz | Must be deterministic and low latency | | GNSS update | 1–20 Hz | Must use fix time, not arrival time | | Camera or lidar update | 5–60 Hz | Processing delay can dominate | | Health monitor | 1–50 Hz | Must detect stale or inconsistent state | | State output to control | 20–200 Hz | Must publish a fresh, timestamped state | | Logging | Sensor rate | Must not block estimator deadlines | : Representative rates in a navigation package. {#tbl-practical-rates} The estimator should measure its own timing and log the result: ```python import time class StepTimer: def __init__(self): self.records_ms = [] def time_step(self, name, fn, *args, **kwargs): start = time.perf_counter() result = fn(*args, **kwargs) elapsed_ms = 1000.0 * (time.perf_counter() - start) self.records_ms.append((name, elapsed_ms)) return result ``` Profiling is not only for optimization. Timing spikes often reveal logging, memory allocation, blocking I/O, or lock contention in places where the estimator should be predictable. Look at the tail of the distribution, not the mean: a step that takes 0.3 ms on average and 40 ms once a minute will drop IMU samples once a minute. Most vehicle systems receive sensors asynchronously. A common pattern is to let sensor drivers, perception front ends, logging, and health monitoring run in separate tasks while the estimator state is protected by a small, explicit critical section. Do expensive work outside the estimator lock: feature tracking, packet parsing, file I/O, and visualization should never block IMU propagation. If a shared lock is held long enough to miss sensor deadlines, the software architecture is part of the navigation error budget now. Long-running Kalman filters also need numerical checks. Force the covariance to stay symmetric after each update, check for NaNs and infinities, confirm that diagonal entries stay positive, and watch for Cholesky failures or a growing condition number. Use the Joseph-form update or a factored (square-root or UD) filter when the filter runs for hours (@sec-kf-joseph-form). None of this rescues a filter with wrong units, wrong signs, or invented measurement covariances; it only keeps a correct filter from being destroyed by rounding. If innovations are persistently large in one direction, do not start by tuning harder. Start by checking frames, lever arms, timestamps, and units. ## From Python Prototype to Embedded Code {#sec-practical-translating-python-prototypes} Python is excellent for learning, plotting, and building reference implementations. It is usually not what runs inside a flight controller or a tightly constrained navigation computer, and moving to C, C++, or Rust changes the engineering problem. | Python prototype | Embedded implementation | |---|---| | Dynamic arrays | Fixed-size arrays where possible | | NumPy hides loops | Loops and memory layout are explicit | | Exceptions are common | Error states are often explicit return values | | Heap allocation is easy | Heap allocation may be banned in real-time paths | | Units live in variable names | Units may need strong types or strict conventions | | Plots are immediate | Diagnostics must be logged and decoded later | : What changes between a Python prototype and embedded code. {#tbl-practical-python-embedded} **Keep the Python version as a reference model.** Do not throw it away after porting. Generate small test vectors from it and compare the embedded outputs within tolerances, function by function: coordinate transforms, quaternion propagation, gravity and Earth rate, process-noise discretization, measurement prediction, the innovation and gain, and covariance symmetry and positive definiteness after updates. **Prefer fixed dimensions.** Many navigation filters have known state and measurement dimensions: a 15-state error model, a 3D position fix, a 6D position-velocity fix. Fixed sizes make timing, allocation, and stack usage easy to reason about. Where the Python prototype lets `np.linalg.solve` discover shapes at runtime, the embedded version should name its dimensions, and like the prototype it should solve linear systems rather than form explicit inverses. **Control memory allocation.** Real-time loops should not allocate memory unpredictably. In C++ that usually means fixed-size Eigen matrices or preallocated buffers; in Rust, stack arrays, fixed-capacity containers, or caller-owned workspaces; in C, being honest about every buffer size and checking every index. If a loop must run at 400 Hz, do not let it discover at runtime that memory allocation is slow today. **Use types to protect conventions.** Many bugs are convention mistakes: seconds versus milliseconds, radians versus degrees, NED versus ENU, body-to-navigation versus navigation-to-body, quaternion component order. C++ and Rust can encode some of these in types (a `Duration` is not a `float`, a `QuatWxyz` is not a `QuatXyzw`); use them where the added complexity buys real safety. At minimum, name variables with units and frames: ```python gyro_radps_b = imu.gyro_radps accel_mps2_b = imu.accel_mps2 position_ned_m = state.position_ned_m ``` This looks fussy until the day it prevents a degree/radian bug from steering a vehicle into the wrong patch of reality. Eigen deserves a specific warning: its quaternion constructor takes `(w, x, y, z)`, but its `coeffs()` storage order is `(x, y, z, w)`, so the same library uses both conventions depending on how you touch it. ## Testing and Validation {#sec-practical-testing-validation} Do not jump from a plot on recorded data to a full autonomous field test. Build a validation ladder. | Level | Purpose | Example | |---|---|---| | Unit tests | Check small math blocks | Quaternion update against a known rotation | | Recorded datasets | Check estimator behavior | Replay a log with GNSS and IMU | | Synthetic faults | Check failure handling | Drop GNSS for 30 s; inject a 50 ms timing error | | Monte Carlo | Check consistency and sensitivity | ANEES over randomized noise and initial errors | | Hardware-in-the-loop | Check I/O and timing | Feed logged IMU and GNSS to the target computer in real time | | Low-risk vehicle tests | Check integration | Slow straight lines, stop-and-go, gentle turns | | Representative field tests | Check real operation | Terrain, vibration, multipath, outages | : The validation ladder. {#tbl-practical-validation-ladder} The early tests should be boring. Stationary tests, straight-line motion, slow turns, known lever arms, and short outages catch many errors before the system gets near a difficult autonomy scenario. If you cannot explain a failure from the logs, add better logs before the next test. Repeating a field test without better instrumentation is usually just collecting more confusion. ### Consistency is a pass/fail test "The estimate looks plausible" is not a test result. Consistency gives numbers with pass/fail bounds (@sec-kf-consistency). In simulation, where truth is known, run $M$ Monte Carlo trials and require the average NEES over the $n$ error states to stay inside its chi-square bounds; with real data, require the time-averaged NIS of each aiding sensor to stay inside its bounds, and the innovations to be white. The bounds are cheap to compute and belong in automated tests: ::: {#practical-consistency-bounds .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} def average_chi2_bounds(dof, n_samples, confidence=0.95): """Two-sided bounds on the average of n_samples independent chi-square(dof) values.""" alpha = 1.0 - confidence lo, hi = chi2.ppf([alpha / 2.0, 1.0 - alpha / 2.0], dof * n_samples) return lo / n_samples, hi / n_samples print("single NEES sample, n = 15: [%.1f, %.1f]" % average_chi2_bounds(15, 1)) print("ANEES, n = 15, M = 50 runs: [%.2f, %.2f]" % average_chi2_bounds(15, 50)) print("time-averaged NIS, m = 3, K = 600: [%.2f, %.2f]" % average_chi2_bounds(3, 600)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` single NEES sample, n = 15: [6.3, 27.5] ANEES, n = 15, M = 50 runs: [13.52, 16.56] time-averaged NIS, m = 3, K = 600: [2.81, 3.20] ``` ::: ::: A single NEES sample of a 15-state filter can land anywhere from about 6 to 27 without anything being wrong, which is why one run proves little. Fifty runs pin the average to within about ±10% of 15, so a covariance that is consistently too small or too large by more than that fails the test. Successive NEES values within one run are correlated, so average across runs at each time step, as @sec-kf-nees-nis does, rather than treating every step of every run as an independent sample. Replay tests on recorded data can assert NIS bounds in the same way, and a regression that pushes NIS out of bounds should fail the build just as surely as a crash. ### Unit tests for navigation components Navigation code is unusually well suited to unit testing, because so much of it has exact answers. Frame conversions must round-trip. A perfect, stationary IMU must leave a full mechanization at rest. A buffer must accept its own edges. With `pytest` (in the course's development dependencies; run with `uv run pytest`), such tests are a few lines each: ```python # tests/test_nav_core.py import numpy as np import pytest from scipy.spatial.transform import Rotation from nav_core.frames import to_ros_odometry, from_ros_odometry from nav_core.strapdown import StrapdownNED, stationary_imu_reading @pytest.mark.parametrize("yaw_deg", [0.0, 30.0, 179.0, -90.0]) @pytest.mark.parametrize("pitch_deg", [-60.0, 0.0, 5.0]) def test_ros_conversion_round_trips(yaw_deg, pitch_deg): x, y, z, w = Rotation.from_euler("ZYX", [yaw_deg, pitch_deg, 3.0], degrees=True).as_quat() q_bn = np.array([w, x, y, z]) p_ned, v_ned = np.array([10.0, -4.0, 2.0]), np.array([1.0, 2.0, -0.5]) ros = to_ros_odometry(p_ned, v_ned, q_bn, np.zeros(3), np.eye(15)) p_back, v_back, q_back = from_ros_odometry(ros) np.testing.assert_allclose(p_back, p_ned, atol=1e-12) np.testing.assert_allclose(v_back, v_ned, atol=1e-12) assert abs(abs(q_back @ q_bn) - 1.0) < 1e-12 # q and -q are the same rotation def test_stationary_imu_stays_put(): """A perfect IMU at rest at WPI: one minute of full mechanization must not move.""" lat, lon, h = np.deg2rad(42.27), np.deg2rad(-71.81), 150.0 ins = StrapdownNED(lat, lon, h, v_ned=np.zeros(3), q_bn=np.array([1.0, 0, 0, 0])) f_b, omega_b = stationary_imu_reading(lat, h, ins.q_bn) # gravity and Earth rate for _ in range(60 * 200): ins.step(f_b, omega_b, dt=1.0 / 200.0) assert np.linalg.norm(ins.v_ned) < 1e-6 assert abs(ins.lat - lat) < 1e-12 ``` The stationary test catches an astonishing range of bugs (a wrong gravity sign, a missing Earth-rate term, transposed rotations) and it runs in well under a second. The flat-Earth drift in @sec-ins-gnss-stationary-demo is exactly what it would catch if someone simplified the mechanization. ### Evaluation evidence Do not reuse a performance table across vehicles, sensors, datasets, or compute platforms. Report a result only together with its truth source, time alignment, environment, configuration, and any excluded segments. The evidence below is a defensible minimum. | Evidence | Question answered | |---|---| | Absolute and relative position and attitude error | How close was the estimate where truth is available? | | NEES (with truth) and NIS (without), against chi-square bounds | Did the uncertainty match the observed errors and residuals? | | Accepted and rejected measurements, with quality flags | Which sensor evidence was trusted, and why? | | State-output age and timing distribution | Was the estimate timely enough for its consumers? | | Outage and fault-injection results | Did uncertainty and health mode respond honestly? | | Deterministic replay | Can the result be reproduced from the same data and configuration? | : Minimum evidence for a navigation performance claim. {#tbl-practical-evidence} The plots that earn their keep are position, velocity, and attitude errors with their ±3σ bounds, estimated biases, innovations with ±3√S bounds and their NIS, accepted versus rejected measurements, latency histograms, and the age of the state at the controller. ## INS Error Behavior in the Real World {#sec-practical-ins-error-behavior} An INS does not fail randomly. It tends to fail in recognizable ways, and knowing them makes field logs much easier to read. ### Bias Drift Accelerometer bias integrates into velocity error and then position error. Gyro bias integrates into attitude error, and attitude error is especially dangerous because it rotates gravity incorrectly: a small tilt projects part of the gravity vector into horizontal acceleration, creating horizontal velocity and position drift (@sec-ins-errors-why-bias-dominates). That is why a stationary IMU test is useful but incomplete. It reveals bias, noise, and warm-up behavior, but it does not excite every error mode that matters on a moving vehicle. ### GNSS Outages During a GNSS outage, the inertial solution should coast and its covariance should grow. If position covariance stays tiny through a long outage, the filter is probably overconfident. That may look clean in a plot until GNSS returns and the innovation is enormous. For testing, deliberately create outages in replay: ```python def hide_gnss_between(samples, start_s, stop_s): """Yield all samples except GNSS fixes in the outage interval.""" for sample in samples: is_gnss = sample.kind == "gnss" in_outage = start_s <= sample.time_s <= stop_s if is_gnss and in_outage: continue yield sample ``` Then check whether the estimator uncertainty grows, whether the return-to-GNSS innovation is plausible (its NIS should be consistent with the grown covariance), and whether the filter recovers without a discontinuity that would surprise the controller. ### Schuler Cycles In a curved-Earth INS, horizontal position and velocity errors couple through the gravity model and local-level frame. The resulting error dynamics include the Schuler period, roughly 84 minutes: $$ T_S \approx 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{R_E}{g}}. $$ For this course, the important point is not to derive every Schuler-mode equation. The important point is to know that inertial error dynamics have physical structure. A high-quality INS does not simply drift as an arbitrary polynomial forever. Earth curvature, gravity, attitude error, and velocity error interact. On a short robot dataset, you may never see a clean Schuler cycle. On marine, aerospace, or long-duration inertial systems, Schuler behavior is part of the background reality. If you work in that domain, read a dedicated strapdown INS text and treat the simplified course implementation as the beginning, not the finish line. ## Common Failure Modes {#sec-practical-common-failure-modes} Most deployed navigation failures are not exotic. They are ordinary mistakes with large consequences. **Timestamp bugs:** measurements are processed at arrival time instead of measurement time, or two clocks are assumed to agree when they do not. **Time-scale bugs:** GPS time and UTC are mixed (18 s), or a replayed log is stamped with the wall clock instead of simulated time. **Frame convention bugs:** ENU and NED are mixed, a rotation is applied in the wrong direction, or a quaternion is read in the wrong component order. **Unit bugs:** milliseconds are used as seconds, degrees as radians, or latitude/longitude differences as meters. **Lever-arm bugs:** GNSS antenna measurements are compared directly to the IMU position even though the antenna is somewhere else on the vehicle, or the lever arm has the wrong sign. **Overconfident covariance:** the filter claims high certainty during outages, after rejected aiding measurements, or because a driver published zeros meaning "unknown." **Bad initialization:** the system starts before gyro bias, attitude, or sensor time offsets are reasonable. **Silent sensor degradation:** GNSS multipath, IMU saturation, vibration, thermal shift, a DVL losing bottom lock, or camera blur enters the estimator as if nothing changed. **Logging gaps:** the system logs state estimates but not raw measurements, configuration, calibration, or rejected updates, making failures impossible to replay. **Controller mismatch:** the controller assumes the state is current, in a different frame, or smoother than the estimator actually provides. These are not glamorous problems. They are also the problems that consume real engineering time. ## Case Study: Navigating a Survey AUV {#sec-practical-case-study} To see the whole contract on one vehicle, consider an autonomous underwater vehicle surveying the seafloor: a torpedo-shaped AUV a few meters long, rated to 3000 m, flying 40 m above the bottom at 2 m/s with a multibeam echosounder and a side-scan sonar, for missions of a day or more. The client wants seafloor features positioned to better than 5 m (95%) in 1500 m of water, along a grid of survey lines tens of kilometers long. GNSS does not penetrate water, so for most of the mission the vehicle is navigating on inertial sensors, a Doppler velocity log, a pressure sensor, and acoustic fixes relayed from its support ship. It is a compact version of every problem in this chapter, and the configuration is typical of operational survey AUVs [@paull2014auv]. ### The sensor suite | Sensor | Measures | Rate | Latency | Frame | Accuracy (typical) | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Navigation-grade INS (fiber-optic gyros) | Δθ, Δv | 200 Hz | < 2 ms | IMU, mounted to body | Gyro bias ~0.01°/h; accel bias ~50 µg | | GNSS, single mast antenna | Position, velocity | 5 Hz, surfaced only | 50–100 ms | Antenna, ~1.2 m above IMU | 1–2 m (SBAS) | | DVL, 600 kHz, four beams | Velocity over the seafloor (bottom track) or through the water (water track); altitude | 4–8 Hz | 50–150 ms | DVL head, rotated ~45° in yaw | 0.2% ± 1 mm/s; bottom lock to ~90 m altitude | | Pressure sensor | Depth | 10 Hz | ~20 ms | Sensor port, ~1 m ahead of IMU | 0.01% of full scale (0.3 m) plus conversion error | | USBL, ship-based, via acoustic modem | AUV position | every 5–10 s | 3–10 s | Ship transducer → ship body → geodetic | A few tenths of a percent of slant range | | Ship INS and dual-antenna GNSS | Ship position, heading, attitude for the USBL | 10–20 Hz | ms | Ship body | Heading a few hundredths of a degree | : Sensor suite for the survey AUV and its support ship. {#tbl-practical-auv-sensors} The last row is on the ship, not the AUV, but it is part of the AUV's navigation system whether or not anyone drew it on the AUV's block diagram. Its 15 error states (position, velocity, attitude, accelerometer and gyro biases) are augmented with a DVL scale factor, three small DVL misalignment angles, a depth sensor bias, and two horizontal water-current components for water-track operation, for 22 in total. A navigation-grade gyro senses Earth rate, so the INS can find north by itself (@sec-ins-gnss-alignment); on a rolling ship's deck it aligns with GNSS aiding instead, and it refines that alignment on the surface before diving. Each sensor enters through its own measurement model. **GNSS** position is a loose update with the antenna lever arm, accepted only when the vehicle is surfaced (depth below 0.3 m, and the receiver reporting a fix not interrupted by waves washing over the mast). **DVL bottom-track** velocity is the body-frame model of @sec-measurement-models-navigation-sensors, with the scale factor, misalignment, and the lever-arm term $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{nb}^b \times \boldsymbol{\ell}_d^b$; because it is resolved in the body frame, it also makes heading drift observable as the vehicle turns at the end of each survey line. **DVL water-track** velocity is the same model minus the current states, used when the bottom is out of range. **Depth** from pressure constrains the vertical channel tightly, which is the best-behaved channel on the vehicle. **USBL** fixes constrain horizontal position; each arrives late and is applied at its time of validity through the buffer, after an NIS gate rejects outliers caused by acoustic multipath off the surface or the ship's hull. Two details trip people up. Depth is measured from the sea surface, not from the WGS-84 ellipsoid, and the two differ by the geoid height (tens of meters) plus the tide, so the filter carries depth in its vertical channel and converts to ellipsoidal height only at the output. And converting pressure to depth depends on water density and gravity: treating a decibar as a meter is wrong by the better part of a percent, more than ten meters at 2000 m, so use the standard seawater formula with latitude. Between USBL fixes, a well-calibrated DVL-aided INS drifts horizontally by a tenth to a few tenths of a percent of distance traveled; across a 10 km survey line that is roughly 10–30 m, which the USBL fixes then pull back. The real-time filter serves the autopilot. The survey product is renavigated afterward with a smoother (@sec-kf-smoothing) that uses every USBL fix, past and future, which is how the final positions meet a specification that the real-time filter alone would not. That is the contract in miniature: two consumers with different needs, and an estimator design that serves both. ### Time-synchronization plan Timing here is forgiving in one way and unforgiving in another. At 2 m/s, a 1 ms timing error is 2 mm of position, and at a 3°/s turn rate it is 0.003° of heading, so millisecond-level synchronization is ample on the AUV. The hard problems are the multi-second latency of the USBL fix and the 100 ms-class latency of the DVL. The plan is as follows. Every computer runs on GPS time internally, with UTC used only in human-readable logs. On deck and at the surface, the navigation computer disciplines its clock to the GNSS receiver's PPS and time messages through `chrony`; the INS stamps its IMU samples with its own PPS-disciplined counter. Submerged, the computer clock free-runs on an oven-controlled oscillator whose drift over a day-long dive is around a millisecond, which the budget above absorbs (an ordinary 20 ppm crystal would drift by more than a second). Where a DVL's output carries its mid-ping time, that is the stamp to use; this vehicle's DVL driver stamps arrival time, so the 84 ms latency in the calibration file of @sec-practical-calibration-configuration-frame was measured by cross-correlating DVL and INS velocities during the calibration run. The USBL fix is stamped on the ship in GPS time at the moment the AUV's transponder replied, which is the time of validity (not the reception time at the ship, and certainly not the time the modem message reached the AUV). The buffer retains 15 s of states and IMU increments, comfortably more than the worst expected fix latency. On the ship side the requirement is much tighter. The USBL solution needs the ship's attitude at the instant of the ping, and in a seaway the ship rolls at several degrees per second. A 10 ms misalignment between the USBL and motion sensor clocks at 4°/s of roll is a 0.04° angle error, which at 1800 m of slant range is more than a meter. That is why USBL installations tie the transceiver and motion sensor to a common PPS. ### Calibration list Before the vehicle is trusted on a survey, the calibration file needs: the IMU mounting rotation and an acceptance-test Allan deviation for each axis; lever arms from the IMU to the DVL, the GNSS antenna, the pressure port, and the USBL transponder, measured with a total station in the workshop; the DVL mounting rotation and scale factor from an in-water calibration run (reciprocal straight lines and a box pattern on the surface with GNSS, which pins the yaw misalignment to a few hundredths of a degree and the scale to about 0.1%); the DVL latency; a pressure-sensor zero taken at the surface before each dive; the sound-speed profile from a CTD cast, used for USBL ray bending; and, on the ship, the USBL transceiver alignment from a dedicated calibration pattern and the ship's own lever arms and timing. The DVL scale and misalignment remain filter states with small process noise, so the calibration run provides good initial values and the filter tracks small changes. ### Output contract to the autopilot The autopilot's depth, pitch, and heading loops have bandwidths well under 1 Hz, so a 50 Hz output with under 20 ms of latency is ample. The navigation node publishes the odom-frame pose (continuous), body-frame velocity, attitude, angular rate, depth, and DVL altitude above the seabed, with covariances, plus the map-to-odom correction and a health message carrying the mode, the active aids, the time since the last USBL fix and since bottom lock was last held, and per-aid NIS flags. Line following shows why the odom/map split matters here. Survey lines are defined in geographic coordinates, so cross-track error is ultimately a map-frame quantity. But a USBL fix can move the map-frame estimate by several meters at once, and a cross-track controller that sees a 4 m step will turn sharply to correct it, putting a kink in the multibeam swath that the post-processing team will remember. The guidance layer therefore applies map-to-odom corrections gradually, rate-limited to a few centimeters per second, and the survey positions are fixed later by the smoother anyway. Terrain safety uses the DVL's altitude measurement and a forward-looking sonar directly, never the navigation position, because the seafloor does not care where the filter thinks it is. ### Degraded modes The vehicle's modes map directly onto @tbl-practical-consumer-actions. **Surfaced with GNSS** is `AIDED`. **Submerged with bottom lock** is `DEAD_RECKONING`, promoted to `AIDED` while USBL fixes are fresh. **Water track** is a weaker `DEAD_RECKONING`: unknown currents make drift grow faster, and the published σ must grow with it. **No DVL at all** is `INERTIAL_ONLY`, which a navigation-grade INS survives for minutes with modest error but not for hours. The policies follow from the survey requirement. If the horizontal σ exceeds the survey tolerance, the sonar data are flagged as out of specification but the line continues. If σ exceeds 25 m, or the vehicle has been inertial-only for more than ten minutes, it abandons the line, holds a safe altitude, and waits for USBL fixes or, if the mission allows, surfaces for GNSS. If bottom lock is lost near the seafloor, the vehicle climbs, because the DVL was also its altimeter. If the USBL NIS monitor alarms, USBL updates are suspended and the operator on the ship is alerted. The descent is a planned degraded mode: for most of the 1500 m descent the bottom is beyond DVL range, so the vehicle navigates on the INS, water track, and USBL, and the plan budgets the horizontal error at the moment bottom lock is acquired. ### Validation plan The validation ladder for this vehicle runs as follows. Unit tests and deterministic replay of earlier missions guard against regressions. A hardware-in-the-loop bench replays recorded INS, DVL, pressure, and USBL data into the navigation computer in real time and checks timing. Dock tests check gyrocompass convergence time and heading against the surveyed heading of the quay. Surface runs with RTK GNSS as truth provide NEES, and replaying them with GNSS masked emulates a dive with a perfect reference. Shallow dives with GNSS fixes before and after give the surfacing error as a percentage of distance traveled, and across many dives the NEES of the surfacing error, which has two horizontal degrees of freedom, should average 2 within its chi-square bounds. Deep trials monitor NIS on every DVL and USBL update and compare the real-time track with the smoothed one. Fault injection in replay covers DVL dropouts, USBL outliers, fixes later than the buffer, and a clock step. Only after all of that does the vehicle go to work, and the logs from its first real survey become the next regression test. ## Practical Checklist {#sec-practical-checklist} Before trusting a navigation system on a vehicle, check the following. - [ ] The estimator replays recorded logs deterministically, from the same data and configuration. - [ ] Raw sensor data, calibrated measurements, state, innovations, accept/reject decisions, health, configuration, and calibration are logged together. - [ ] Every measurement has a documented frame, unit, and time of validity. - [ ] The estimator runs on one continuous time scale; GPS time and UTC are never mixed; intervals come from a monotonic clock. - [ ] Clocks are synchronized (PPS, PTP, or triggering) or their offsets and drifts are estimated, and constant sensor time offsets are calibrated. - [ ] Delayed measurements are applied at their own time through a state buffer, a delayed fusion horizon, or an OOSM update. - [ ] Extrinsics, lever arms, time offsets, and noise settings live in one versioned calibration file, with sign conventions written next to the numbers; everything else is generated from it. - [ ] Every conversion between conventions (NED/ENU, FRD/FLU, quaternion order, degrees/radians) is named and unit-tested. - [ ] Covariance grows during outages; published covariances are never constants or zeros; NIS monitors run on every aid. - [ ] Large innovations are gated, counted, and logged. - [ ] Joseph form or a factored filter is used for long-running filters, with symmetry and NaN checks. - [ ] The output carries a time of validity, frames, covariance, and a health message with mode, active aids, and time since the last absolute fix. - [ ] Controllers receive a continuous state (or are told about resets); planners receive a globally consistent one. - [ ] Every consumer has its own watchdog on the age of the navigation state. - [ ] Consistency (ANEES in simulation, NIS on data) is part of the automated tests. - [ ] The embedded implementation is tested against the Python reference on small numerical cases. - [ ] Field tests begin with stationary, straight-line, and low-speed maneuvers before aggressive autonomy. The goal is not to make anyone afraid of implementation. The goal is to make the boundary visible. A navigation algorithm is the mathematical center of the system, but a navigation package is a real-time software product wrapped around sensors, calibration, timing, logging, health monitoring, and contracts with the vehicle. Integration is harder than a block diagram because it forces every hidden assumption to become an interface, a timestamp, a calibration record, or a test, and that wrapper is where many real systems succeed or fail. ## Exercises {#sec-practical-exercises} 1. **A time-sync and output contract for a delivery drone.** A quadrotor delivers parcels at up to 15 m/s.
